maintopic: IMMIGRATION ACT AMENDMENT.
IMMIGRATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: LEWIS moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 135) to amend the Immigration Act-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: IMMIGRATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The first section directs that immigrants when they land in this country shall be examined for weapons which the citizens of Canada are not allowed to carry,
and that each immigrant shall be furnished with a printed document in his own language explaining to him, as shall also be done viva voce, that he shall not be allowed to carry such weapons. The first thing an immigrant after landing sees displayed in the windows of the second-hand stores of the port, are rows of revolvers, dirks, knives, and other weapons which ordinary Canadians are not permitted to use; and consequently he imagines that in this to him wild western country it is necessary for him to be armed with some of these weapons. The second section is an addition to the Bill I brought in before, and is in the line of the few remarks I made in the debate on the address at the beginning of this session, as to the class of immigrants that should be allowed to land in this country; and it reads as follows:
From and after the first day of January, 1911, natives of Europe south of 44 degrees north latitude and east of 20 degrees east longitude, and natives of Turkey in Asia, shall be prohibited from entering in and settling in Canada.
I contend that this country should in this respect take warning by the example of that great country to the south of us. Originally the slavery question was a very heavy and dark looking question to the citizens of the United States; but that question is overshadowed by another serious menace in the immigration of people from Southern Europe. Reports state that the average citizen of the United States is deteriorating physically, mentally and morally, of course on the average taking in all foreigners. Sir. we do not want immigrants to come here to hew our wood, draw our water, plough our 6elds and dig our coal alone. We want them to be one with the happy, free and independent citizens of Canada in forming a nation; and I contend that the only yay to do this is to keep out all people except those of western Europe who have the same hereditary as ourselves.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

maintopic: IMPROVED PAPER MACHINERY COMPANY.

speechtext:
House in Committee on Bill (No. 67) respecting the Improved Paper Machinery Company.-Mr. Worthington.
On section 1,
Power to Commissioner of Patents to re-" ceive fee and extend duration of patent.

maintopic: IMPROVED PAPER MACHINERY COMPANY.
speechtext:
Unfortunately I was not present when the Bill was before the Committee on Private Bills. May I, therefore, ask the hon. member who has charge of this Bill (Mr. Worthington) to explain the reasons for asking for this legislation. Perhaps I may be permitted to say, we have a
great many applications to parliament in recent years to renew patents which have become void for one reason or another. A Bill was passed a short time ago concerning a case in which the trouble, I am told, arose from the fact that, though the amount necessary for the renewal had been sent to the bank of Montreal, yet, through the mistake of a clerk, it was not forwarded to the patent office. In such a case, it is only reasonable, perhaps, that the patent should be renewed. What I particularly would like to know, in the present case, is whether the patentee commenced manufacturing within two years, and otherwise complied with the patent law. And, was the difficulty simply an omission to pay the fee within the time-which, I understand, expired on January 26, 1909-or is this a case in which a patent has become void, making this a Bill merely to give back rights which the patentee has forfeited through his own negligence to comply with the law?

maintopic: IMPROVED PAPER MACHINERY COMPANY.
speechtext: This Bill was before the Committee on Private Bills at its last meeting and was accepted by the committee with the concurrence of the Minister of Agriculture. This was an exceptional case in which the holder of the patent was not responsible for the lapse of the patent.

maintopic: IMPROVED PAPER MACHINERY COMPANY.
speechtext: What were the circumstances?

maintopic: IMPROVED PAPER MACHINERY COMPANY.
speechtext: This is a very large company which has a solicitor employed especially for the purpose of keeping these patents in force. Through the negligence of this solicitor, one patent was allowed to lapse-it was misplaced. The solicitor recognized that the fault was his own, and offered to compensate the company. The company has built a large plant at Sherbrooke-it is one of Sherbrooke's largest industries-and is now prepared to manufacture this improved paper machinery, in fact has begun to do it.

maintopic: IMPROVED PAPER MACHINERY COMPANY.
speechtext: Did they begin ihe manufacture within two years from the granting of their patent?

maintopic: IMPROVED PAPER MACHINERY COMPANY.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: IMPROVED PAPER MACHINERY COMPANY.
speechtext: In Canada?

maintopic: IMPROVED PAPER MACHINERY COMPANY.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: IMPROVED PAPER MACHINERY COMPANY.
speechtext: If this has passed under the cognizance of the Minister of Agriculture, I think that is the main thing.

maintopic: IMPROVED PAPER MACHINERY COMPANY.
speechtext:
The Minister of Agriculture took the case into consideration and decided that it was an exceptional case in which the company was not to blame, and for that reason the Bill should be allowed to pass, with the understanding that a proviso at the end of the Bill should be withdrawn.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.

speechtext:
House in Committee on Bill (No. 80) to incorporate L'Institut de Notre Dame des Missions.-Mr. W. M. Martin.
On section 7, subsection 2, as amended:
The annual value of the real estate held in Canada by or in trust for the corporation shall not exceed fifty thousand dollars.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: What does that mean- ' the annual value of the real estate?' Will the hon. member who has charge of the Bill please explain?

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: In the Committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills it was pointed out that the power to hold real estate to the value of only $50,000 was very little in the case of a corporation such as this. Especially is this the case when you consider the relative values of real estate in western Canada and in eastern Canada. The object of the amendment in this case, as I understand it, is to allow the corporation to hold property which will produce an annual revenue of $50,000.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: That would be a pretty large estate.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: When it is considered that this corporation, or voluntary society, at the present time holds real estate in something like eleven different places in the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, it will be seen that it does not need to hold much in each place to make a total holding of $50,000 annually. And, from my own personal knowledge of this society, I can say that it will not take very many holdings such as they have at the present time to make a total value of three or four hundred thousand annually.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: An annual value of $50,000 represents about $1,250,000 capital value.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Money in the west is worth 7 per cent if not 8 per cent, and if you figure it on that basis it only makes about $700,000.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: This is not a land company, is it?

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: In order to carry out the purposes for which they are incorporated it is necessary' for them to hold land. I know they have acquired land in Regina, worth many thousand dollars and they have lately let a contract in that city for the building of a convent which will cost probably $50,000 or $60,000.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Under what charter have they been conducting their business in the other western provinces?

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: I am informed they have a charter in Manitoba which was granted about 1882 and under which they have been operating up to the present time. They have no charter in Alberta or Saskatchewan, and it is the intention to operate under the proposed new charter in all the western provinces.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Why should it not come under the provincial government?

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: They would have to have three or four different charters.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Inasmuch as the control of education belongs to the different provinces, should not this charter be obtained from the provincial government? I ask the Prime Minister what the rule is?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: I have not looked into the Bill and I am not prepared to express an opinion on it. It is private legislation.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Was the question of provincial rights brought up in the committee? Would it not be better in matters of this kind that are purely within the jurisdiction of the provinces, that the local legislatures should deal with them? As I understand, the Bill simply asks authority to do business in the new provinces, not in any other part of Canada, and if that be the case why should they not obtain a charter from the provincial legislature?

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: All these institutions are after government grants for education; they will naturally be under the control of the provinces in relation to education; they should be inspected by provincial inspectors, they are subject to provincial laws in relation to provisions for safety, &c., and if we grant charters to institutions of this kind, we are trespassing on the rights of the provinces in these matters. The whole control of matters relating to education should be left in the hands of the provinces as it is a provincial matter relating to the education of the youth of the country. I think the Bill has no place in this parliament.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: This is clearly an interprovincial Bill. This corporation, as it will be, is not asking anything more from this parliament than any railway corporation does when it asks for the privilege of building lines connecting two or three provinces. We cannot be expected to go into every province in the Dominion where we want to carry on business and ask a charter. We decided to come to this parliament and ask a Dominion charter. There is nothing in the Bill dealing with provincial rights, and if my hon. friend from Peel will go into the western provinces, he will find there is no question of provincial rights there to-day.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: I am not stirring up any question of provincial rights, my hon. friend is doing that by the manner in which he refers to it. This should come clearly within the province of the provincial government, and the Dominion parliament should not be asked to grant charters of this kind.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend will see by section 11 that is all provided for.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Yes, I saw that.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend will see that this company must come here to get this charter, they cannot get it elsewhere. No legislature can give a charter for the incorporation of a company to operate in another province, that is interprovincial. This corporation propose to operate in three different provinces, and therefore must come here.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: I understand they have been doing business in Manitoba under a local charter.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Yes, but now they want to extend and they have a right to come here and get this charter.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: In section 7 power is asked to purchase or otherwise acquire certain kinds of property, and it speaks of real or personal and corporeal or incorporeal property. What is incorporeal property?

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: I suppose what is usually meant, bonds, securities and mortgages.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Would that not be considered personal property?

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: I have no objection to changing the word to personal.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: It looks as though it might refer to angels floating in the air, or something of that kind. I do not see what kind of property could be called incorporeal, when you have real and personal and almost every other kind mentioned.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: It would seem to me that the proper wording for subclause 2 would be to state the amount of real estate they may hold. You introduce an element of difference and possibly of some difficulty by not giving a statement of the annual value of the real estate they may hold. If you have any basis on which to calculate it, calculate it on that basis.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Say not exceeding

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: And I think you should say the value of real estate ' so held.' That is for the purposes of the corporation as shown in the preceding clauses. I do not suppose you intend this to become a land dealing company.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Under this clause they could become a banking or loan society or a land speculating institution, [DOT] they could do anything they had a mind to. I would move that this Bill stand over in order that it may receive more careful consideration than it has. It is- a very dangerous Bill from many points of view. In the first place I maintain it conflicts with provincial rights, inasmuch as it is incorporating by the Dominion government an institution for the education of the youth of the country. That is clearly in violation of provincial rights. They can go to the provincial government and obtain their charter. Personally I have objection to incorporating any institutions of this kind under Dominion charters; the province is the proper place for that, in order that they may be subject to proper provincial inspection. All schools are supposed to be subject to provincial inspection, whether they are private or public schools. If we grant this charter we place this school outside of the control or discipline of the province and they will be under no obligation to observe the laws of the province except under one clause, in relation to the control of property. I do not think the Bill should pass until it has received more careful consideration. We all know that when Bills affecting any religious corporation are brought before the House, like this Sunday Observance Bill that we had before parliament a few days ago, we are told that the church is behind them and we stand to one side. I do not think that a Bill of this kind should be allowed to be enacted by this House and I therefore oppose it.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: I do not see how the reasoning of my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) would apply to a case like this. The* moment the fact is indicated to us that this society intends extending its operations beyond one province, we have the jurisdiction to incorporate it.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: It has institutions in two provinces.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext:
It has institutions operating in two provinces, as my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) says, and it may wish to extend its charitable and religious institutions beyond the limits of one province. Therefore, why should we not have power to incorporate it here? We could not incorporate, strictly speaking, a society of that kind intending to operate only in one province. I do not think we could give it legal entity. As a matter of fact we are incorporating this society and placing it under the clear jurisdiction of the province with respect to educational matters. Surely my hon. and gallant friend from Haliburton and Victoria will not deny that? What is the abject of this society? Its object is to do educational,

charitable and other eleemosynary work. Would my hon. friend say that this places it above the laws of the province in respect to education? Surely it is absolutely subject to its laws in the same way as an individual or a purely provincial creation would be. Therefore, it seems to me that the objection of my hon. and gallant friend is not well taken." There is no privilege conferred by this Bill beyond it. It indicates the object of this new creation. It falls consequently under all the laws of the province respecting education, and if it went beyond in any respect it would be unconstitutional.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: I am very much impressed by the statement of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). I think that if the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) would consider the course he is taking in this matter he would see that this is not education as it is referred to in section 93 of the British North America Act. That refers to public education; this is a purely private matter. The applicants for this Bill wish to educate their children, or rather provide institutions at which children may be educated, but it is purely private. It has nothing to do with public education and it has nothing to do with education in the sense in which it is referred to by the British North America Act. I would call my hon. friend's attention.to the fact that many bodies have been incorporated by this parliament with practically the same objects in view as those for which this Bill is introduced, and if it be true that these applicants wish to do business in all of the provinces of Canada excepting Manitoba, they are practically compelled to come here. The society might possibly get one charter in Saskatchewan and another in Alberta, but there would be no possibility of working them under one general head. It would be two distinct corporations. In going over the provisions of this Bill it will be seen that they are similar to the provisions of a Bill passed by this parliament in 1884, one with which the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton will not quarrel, and that was a Bill for the incorporation of the Methodist Church of Canada. The Methodist Church of Canada consisted probably of corporations in each of the provinces as far as I know. All these different corporations were banded together in one and very much the same provisions were incorporated in the Bill as were asked for in this Bill. This Bill gives this corporation the right to hold property.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: As I understand that Bill was to amalgamate certain different religious bodies into one.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Exactly, and so does this.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Absolutely so. There is a body in Manitoba that has a corporate right, there is a body in Saskatchewan which has no corporate right, and there is property held by different persons in trust for these bodies. There is another body in Alberta holding property in trust. But the same principle is involved in each case; they are trying to get these three bodies incorporated under a general head and there is provision by which they may hold property, borrow money on their property, and the parties who hold property in trust are authorized to convey it to this corporation. It seems to me that is exactly the power that the .Methodist Church got. I think that the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton, if he considers_ these matters, will say that if it is fair in. one case it is fair in the other. The only thing I would suggest would be an amendment to clause 2 of section 7. It is, to my mind, unreasonable to limit the holdings of this society to $50,000. I do not know what amount would be proper, but the hon. gentleman who has charge of the Bill can state what, in his opinion, would be a proper amount. With that change, it seems to me, the Bill is not only necessary for the work, but it is perfectly legitimate and it should pass.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext:
The parallel which has been drawn by the hon. member for Car-leton, New Brunswick, (Mr. Carvell) does not hold. Unless I can get some further legal knowledge from the two brilliant legal minds which have just preceded me, I must still hold to my view that this Bill clearly trangresses the rights and duties of . the provinces. 'The Bill declares that:
The objects of the corporation shall be the instruction and the Christian education of children and other works of charity, such as work rooms

This is a bad piece of composition, I should imagine, but the objects can be very well understood

-orphanages, refuges and other similar undertakings, and the advancement, in other ways, of education and religion, charity and benevolence.
These are all very proper, but the education of the youth of the land comes clearly under the power of the provincial authorities, and the point 1 want made clear to my mind is that if this Bill is passed in its present form will the provinces have any

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman mean to convey to the committee the idea that the private education of pupils, or the conduct of private schools, comes, under the British North America Act, within the jurisdiction of the local government?

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: There is no private educational institution in Ontario, or in any other province of the Dominion of Canada, but is under inspection by the

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext:
'I would like my hon. friend to answer the question.
Mr. HUGHES Just let my hon. friend wait until I am finished and he will get his answer. There is not one which is not, under the law, under inspection for fire purposes, for educational purposes and for other purposes.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Look at section 11.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: For educational purposes they are under the control of the provinces

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Section 11 says that all provincial laws apply.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend from Victoria and Haliburton seems to conjure up something that is not here at all. I know he has strong views with respect to education, but he would deprive school children of a Christian education because he will not permit it in the public school, and he wishes to shut out such education from private schools. We have these private schools in every province in Canada under all denominations. These applicants are here simply to ask for incorporation.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Are the private schools to which my hon. friend refers under Dominion charter?

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Some might very well be.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Mount Allison is.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: We have in New Brunswick, as my hon. friend from Car-leton says, Mount Allison in Sackville, in the county of Westmorland. I see no reason why any of them should not come to this parliament and ask for incorporation. Such an institution as the University of Acadia in Wolfville, in Nova Scotia, does not operate beyond the confines of that province. They do not need any Dominion charter, but, this society purposes operating in at least three of the provinces and, therefore, they should have incorporation from this parliament. In section 11 we say that the exercise of its powers shall be subject to the laws of any province it may operate in, as to the acquisition and holding of land by religious corporations in so far as such laws apply, but even without that I think it would be subject to provincial law's in that respect. It does seem that the point taken by the hon. member (Mr. Foster) with respect to the extent of the value of the property is opportune and that there is ambiguity as to what ' annual value ' means.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: After such a disquisition trom the learned authority on divinity matters-

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: You are convicted.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: A gentleman who is so well posted on all the needs of religious corporations, who has gone to Sunday School, and has had all the benefits of a Christian education as exemplified in his life and bearing, I would be bold indeed to appear to hesitate to accept his conclusions. But, section 11 only applies to the holding of land by religious corporations, and I am not speaking of the holding of lands at all. What I want to know is: If these institutions are formed in a province and should there be public schools, will the children attending them be subject to inspection under the laws of the province? If that is made clear, I have no objection to the Bill. But I require something better than the authority of the learned law lecturer from Laval, or of the luminary from the valley of 'St. John, or of the divinity expert from Westmorland, to convince me of that.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: These are private schools, and should they become public schools, it is for the people of the western provinces to look after them. Until my hon. friend can show that they are public schools, his argument amounts to nothing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Education is under the control of the provinces in relation to public schools which are maintained by taxation. But, in all British countries it is the privilege of British subjects to maintain their own schools if they do not want to send their children to the public schools. In some countries children are compelled to go to public schools, but in British countries parents have the privilege of sending their children to private schools, and that right has never been denied. There are many such private schools in the provinces where nothing but public schools prevail under the authority of the province. But with those voluntary private schools there is no interference, and I do not think this Bill departs from the principle acknowledged in all British countries.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: I am content if there is nothing in this Bill which will interfere with these schools being liable to the province, just the same as if they had a provincial charter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext:
If these schools become public schools they will be under the control of the province, and so far as education is concerned, no authority other than the province has a right to control them.
Mi'. DANIEL. I am not a lawyer, but I do feel that the arguments of the hon. member (Mr. Carvell), and the hon. mem-



ber (Mr. Emmerson) have not convinced me. The hon. member (Mr. Carvell) said that Mount Allison University had a Dominion charter because it operates in more than one province.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman misunderstood me. I say that the Methodist institution at Sackville is managed under a Dominion charter because it is the property of the Methodist Church of Canada, which is incorporated by this parliament. maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: As I understand it the Universities of McGill and Laval have provincial charters and yet they operate throughout the whole Dominion. speechtext: I have not said that Mount Allison University was incorporated by the federal parliament.

speechtext: I have said it is controlled- by the Methodist Church which has a Dominion charter.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: I am referring to the university and not to the church. I have been trying to get a straight answer, but the hon. member (Mr. Carvell) appears to be too good a lawyer to be able to give me such an answer. Does the hon. gentleman refuse to answer the question, yes or no?

speechtext: I have answered it three times already.

speechtext:
As to the merits of this Bill, I have nothing to say, but I do believe that if there is nothing to be said in its favour other than what has been said by the hon. members for Carleton and, Westmorland, then, the reasons for its in-Mr. DANIEL.
corporation by this parliament are very weak indeed. I would still like to inquire what is the nature of ' incorporeal property,' because I think that if there is no such thing we had better strike out these words.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: I would suggest that if the hon. member sends to the library for any law dictionary, he will have no difficulty in the finding the meaning of ' incorporeal property.' It is elementary.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: If it is elementary, the hon. gentleman might give us the information. I have read in Shakespeare of ' incorporeal spirits,' but I have not heard of ineoporeal property.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Might I ask if it is within the authority of this parliament to incorporate incorporeal property? I did not know that our authority extended beyond the confines of the nether world.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: I do not think there is anything in the British North America Act about incorporeal property.

speechtext: The language of subsection 1 is very broad and very peculiar. I beg to move that it be amended so as to read in the last line: 'for the uses and purposes of the corporation.' speechtext: It is like many words lawyers use-it does neither harm nor good.

speechtext: That is when they charge by the word?

speechtext: Suppose property were willed to this institution in opposition to the laws of a province, would its charter override the law's of the province?

speechtext: I have been looking up the word ' incorporeal,' and I wish to give the House the authority.

' not consisting of matter, not having a material body, immaterial.' I do not see any good in putting anything immaterial into this Bill. Then, as relating to law, it says: 'Existing only in contemplation of law, not capable of actual visible seizing or

possession, not being an object of sense, intangible.' If that is the meaning of the word, I think we might better leave it out entirely, and let the rest of the clause translate itself.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: Will the promoter of the Bill please explain the meaning of this term? We should treat all these corporations on the same basis, as they are neither kickable nor damnable.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: I move that the words ' corporeal or incorporeal ' be omitted from clause 7.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: I object to the usual legal phraseology that is used in granting powers to corporations being cut out of this, particular section. These words are found in many similar Bills, as I could show if I had time to look them up. There is certainly no harm done in leaving them in the Bill.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: There are a number of minor legal authorities in the House. There is the law lecturer for Laval; I would like to hear his view on the matter.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: I am not prepared to take part in the discussion.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: I am informed on good authority that the young legal luminary from Regina, brilliant as he may be in politics, is not an authority in law, when he says that ' corporeal or incorporeal ' are words used in a Bill in relation to property.

maintopic: LTNSTITUT DE NOTRE DAME DES MISSIONS.
speechtext: If my hon. friend will take ..the trouble to post himself, he will find that all property is divided into corporeal and incorporeal, and that division has existed for a thousand years. I object to striking out legal phraseology which is used in other acts of incorporation.

If the legal members of the House, or any other members, will tell us what these -words mean, I have no objection to withdraw my amendment. But nobody seems able to tell us that they mean anything. The dictionary says they mean nothing. They are immaterial.

speechtext: Mr. CONMEE moved the second reading of Bill (No. 119) to incorporate the International Waterways Canal and Construction Company.

speechtext: I think that as I raised some objection to this Bill when it was last under consideration, I ought to make a reference to what I understand is the present position of the Bill so far as the promoter is concerned. My hon. friend who has charge of the Bill (Mr. Conmee) has recognized the force of some of the objections which I raised to the Bill and he has authorized me to state to the House, and has said that he would state it also if necessary, that when the Bill goes to the committee he will state that he is quite willing to withdraw some of the objectionable provisions of the Bill, more particularly with regard to the Saskatchewan river being included, and also in regard to the definition of the word ' canal ' which he admits is altogether too broad. As there are some features of the Bill which might with advantage be adopted, and as the public interest may be served by incorporating a company with proper safeguards, I think it might be as well to let the Bill pass the second reading and go to a committee where all parties interested may be heard. They are desirous of being heard and before the committee they and all other parties interested will have that opportunity. Having made these remarks I shall not further press any. objection to the second reading.

maintopic: INTERNATIONAL WATERWAYS CANAL AND CONSTRUCTION COMPANY.
speechtext: I would like to have a definite announcement of the time when the Bill will come before the Railway Committee because the people have been writing and telephoning to me, objecting strongly to the passing of the Bill. both Port Arthur and Fort William and will be glad to send them to any other places or interests of which I can learn.

maintopic: INTERNATIONAL WATERWAYS CANAL AND CONSTRUCTION COMPANY.
speechtext: I entirely agree with what the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) says with regard to the objection that he has to this Bill from several points of view. Coupled with the interference with the Saskatchewan river there are several interests which are affected by some of the extraordinary powers asked for by this Bill, and, therefore, I would ask the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) to see that the date for the hearing of the Bill in committee is so fixed that all parties may have an opportunity to be heard. The powers asked for are of the widest possible nature, very much too broad, and inasmuch as the public and other interests do not seem to be safeguarded in any way, I think that the Bill calls for the severest criticism and the greatest caution. I would ask whether the Bill containing the amendments will be reprinted and distributed amongst members so that we can judge of the extent to which the hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy River proposes to moderate his Bill, because I hope the amendments will have the effect of moderating and not enlarging the scope of the powers asked for.

Nothing in this Act shall be held to give the company a power or exclusive right to or over any water area, river, stream, lake, channel, or over any water privilege not * made, erected or constructed, or in course of construction by the company. All water areas, lakes, rivers, streams or water privileges affected by this Act that are not made, constructed, or in course of construction by the company shall remain in the same position in every respect as if this Act had not been passed.
I think that will remove any ground for such observations as fell from the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Boyce) to the effect that the Bill gives this company too wide privileges. I venture the statement that he will not find on the statute books
anywhere a Bill incorporating either a .railway or a canal company which has as many good safeguards as are to be found in this Bill.

speechtext: I do not care whether that interpretation is there or not. I do [DOT]not see what good it is; the lawyers put it there; I did not.

maintopic: INTERNATIONAL WATERWAYS CANAL AND CONSTRUCTION COMPANY.
speechtext: I am probably as familiar as any hon. member in the House outside of my hon. friend (Mr. Conmee) with the differences of opinion that have arisen as to water-powers in that vicinity. In the provincial legislature we had for a good many years disputes as to certain companies incorporated to develop Keke-beka Falls and the Kaministiqua river, and I point that out as a reason why the people in that vicinity might like to be heard on a Bill such as this. I have expressed no opinion on this Bill; I shall defer that until it is considered in committee, but I think we had better have the proposed amendmertts reprinted so that we will all know what they are. It will not take long and it will not cost much and it will be in the public interest. I have gone further than some gentlemen in the House may think proper in having Bills that are of a public nature referred to some committee so that the people interested may get a chance to be heard. I have not fol-, lowed parliamentary practice in that respect, but we are representing all the people here, and where there are interests involved it is well to give the people a chance to express their views. The chairman of the Railway Committee has taken that view and has fixed days for hearing the people interested in a certain Bill before the committee even though they themselves have not asked to be heard. I think you will find that the chairman of the committee will invite the representatives of any municipality interested to be present at a certain day so as to enable them to state their views. Already we have had communications from Fort William with respect to this Bill, and I think it would not be wise to proceed with it until that municipality has an opportunity to be represented, if it so desires. I think the Bill should be reprinted.

maintopic: INTERNATIONAL WATERWAYS CANAL AND CONSTRUCTION COMPANY.
speechtext: Do I understand the minister to say that this Bill shall be reprinted before it comes before the Railway Committee. Why not have it reprinted before it is referred to the committee so that we may know what we are doing?

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
1.	What communication was addressed by the government to the premiers of the several provinces with reference to the appointment of a Commission on Technical Education?
2.	What replies were received from the premiers of the several provinces?

maintopic: QUESTIONS.
speechtext:
1.	The following communication was addressed by the government to the premiers of the several provinces:
Minister of Labour, Canada.
Ottawa, December 13, 1909.
Dear Sir,-The Dominion government is considering the advisability of appointing a Royal Commission to inquire into the needs and present equipment of the Dominion as respects industrial training and technical education, and into the systems and methods of technical instruction obtaining in other countries, particularly in Great Britain, France, Germany and the United States. It is intended that the commission shall be solely for the purpose of gathering information, the information when obtained, to be published in a suitable report to be at the disposal of the provinces and available for general distribution.
I may say that the view of the government is that a commission of the kind suggested might render valuable services to the Dominion as a whole, since it would be in a position to conduct an inquiry on a wider and more comprehensive scale than might be considered desirable or possible in the case of the different provinces, and which if undertaken by the provinces individually must lead inevitably to the duplication and reduplication of energy and expense.
It is recognized, however, that the work of such a commission, to be of national service, should have the hearty endorsation of the governments of the several provinces of the Dominion, and I am, therefore, writing to ask if the appointment by the federal authorities of a commission of the character and scope suggested would meet with the approval of your government, and to inquire, in particular, inasmuch as some doubt has been expressed on the point, whether exception to

objection to the appointment of such a commission.
Please accept, sir, the expression of my highest regard,
(Sgd.) LOMER GOTJIN,
Prime Minister.
Office of the Prime Minister and President of the Council, Ontario.
Toronto, December 16, 1909. Hon. W. Mackenzie King,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Out.
Dear Sir,-I have your letter of the 13th instant.
I understand the object of the proposed commission, to inquire into the needs and present equipment of the Dominion as respects training and technical education and into the system of methods for technical instruction obtaining in other countries, will be solely for the purpose of gathering information. This being so, I see no objection to the creation of the commission, and no exception will be taken to it on the part of the province of Ontario.
Tours very truly,
(Sgd.) J. P. WHITNEY.
Province of Manitoba, Premier's Office, Winnipeg, December 16, 1909. Hon. W. Mackenzie King,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Ont.
Sir,-I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of yours under date of December 13th, regarding the advisability of appointing a royal commission to inquire into the industrial training and technical education of Canada.
I appreciate the fact that education is a matter under the constitution entirely vested in the provinces and realize that it is a delicate question on which to give advice such as you solicit.
The matter is an important one and I think, in view of the rapid strides along industrial lines that the Canadian people are making, there is necessity for more attention being given to technical education than what has been the practice or custom in the past.
I shall certainly be pleased to see more interest taken in this matter and our young men better qualified for the opportunities that are offered along industrial lines by having a first-class technical education to qualify them for the responsible and important positions that are awaiting men of that quality.
I have the honour to be, sir, -Tour obedient servant,
(Sgd.) R. P. ROBLIN, Premier.
Executive Council, Saskatchewan,
Regina, December 21, 1909. Hon. W. Mackenzie King,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. King,-I have duly received your letter of December 13 on the subject of technical education and the proposal now under consideration by your government for institut-Mr. MACKENZIE KING.
ing an inquiry by a royal commission and which asks whether the proposal meets with the approval of the Saskatchewan government and whether any exception would be taken by us on the ground of jurisdiction.
I may very readily state that the Saskatchewan government will raise no objection against the proposed inquiry by the Dominion government on any grounds; on the contrary we believe that the federal'government is the proper authority to'proceed in the matter in the way proposed, that it is a subject which can be more efficiently, economically and effectively dealt with by the central government than by the various provincial governments; and, in addition that, inasmuch as industrial training and technical instruction intimately affect trade and commerce, these branches of edu-' cation ought to be viewed from the national rather than from the provincial standpoint. Believe me,
Very sincerely yours,
(Sgd.) WALTER SCOTT.
Premier's Office, Alberta,
Edmonton, Alta., December 28, 1909. Hon. W. Mackenzie King,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,-I am instructed by the Hon. Premier Rutherford to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 13th in reference to the advisability of the Dominion government appointing a royal commission to inquire into the needs and present equipment of the Dominion as respects industrial training and technical education.
I am directed by the premier to say that this project meets with the hearty endorsation and approval of his government. .
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) M. J. MACLEOD,
Clerk Executive Council.
Government of the Province of British Columbia, Premier's Office,
Victoria, January 15, 1910. Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Out.
Dear Sir,-I beg to confirm my telegram to you of January 10th as follows:-
Owing to absence of Minister of Education with whom I wished to confer, regret being unable to reply sooner to your favour regarding technical education. He has now returned and an answer will be sent you promptly.
Having since then had an opportunity of consulting with the Minister of Education, I beg to state that the appointment of a commission by the Dominion to inquire into the subject of industrial training and technical instruction meets with the approval of this government.
It is not the intention of the government of this province to take exception to the course you propose on any grounds of jurisdiction.
I might add that this government will gladly afford any facilities in its power to assist in carrying out the object in view.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) RICHARD McBRIDE.

maintopic: WINTER COMMUNICATION WITH PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND.
WINTER COMMUNICATION WITH PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND.
speechtext:
WARBURTON (Queens), moved:
Bor a copy of all memorials, reports, correspondence and documents not already brought down, including report of survey made during the past summer and autumn of the harbour at Cape John and Tatama-gouclie bay, in the counties of Pictou and Colchester, in the province of Nova Scotia, relating to the route of the winter steamers between Prince Edward Island and the mainland of Canada, and suggesting and recommending a change or changes in the said route, and an increase in the number of trips daily of such winter steamers; and also, a copy of all memorials, reports, correspondence and documents relating to the route of the summer mail steamers between Charlottetown and the mainland of Canada, and suggesting a change or changes in that route, and an increase in the number of trips daily of such summer mail steamers; and also with regard to connecting such suggested new summer route or routes with a point or points on the Intercolonial railway, and also, for a copy of all memorials, and correspondence, asking for additional and improved aids to navigation of the harbour of Charlottetown and in Tatamagouche bay and harbour.
He said: Mr. Speaker, before the Christmas vacation I had several short interviews with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) in connection with this route and the steamer service. It was the desire of that hon. gentleman to be present when this motion came up, but, owing to his very regrettable illness, it will not be possible this session, I take it, for him to be present within the time when this motion must be brought forward, if it is to be dealt with at all. The importance to us in Prince Edward Island of this matter of winter communication can hardly be realized, perhaps, by those who do not labour under the disadvantages to which we are subjected through the lack of communication which sometimes exists. I spoke on this question last session, on motion to go into supply, and pointed out that the several governments that had existed since we came into confederation, Conservative and Liberal alike, have made repeated,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: WINTER COMMUNICATION WITH PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND.
speechtext:
sincere and energetic efforts to overcome the difficulties with which they have to contend in regard to winter communication. Briefly, I may say that these efforts began almost the very year-if not the very year -when we entered into confederation. The Mackenzie government put on the route a vessel called the * Albert/ as a test. It was not possible at that early period to procure a boat built for the purpose of ice breaking, and the 'Albert' was a test pending the time when a proper boat could be procured. The 'Albert', which was not much of a success, was succeeded by the ' Northern Light,' built at Quebec, built of wood, sheathed with green-heart wood. The ' Northern Light,' while not well adapted to the work, proved, nevertheless, a very excellent experiment, because, while she was not able to do the work very well, the experience gained from hei performances enabled the government, or the government's marine advisers, to design a vessel which did good work later on; and so the 'Northern Light' may be called a very successful experiment. She was followed by the ' Stanley.' This was under the Conservative government. This vessel did good work. Ten or twelve years ago the ' Minto ' was put on, and both these vessels continued on the route up to last year. Both these vessels did very good work, but they were not sufficiently strong to maintain the service during certain seasons of the year and under certain weather conditions. Last year, a new ship, the ' Earl Grey ' was put on. She is a much larger and more powerful vessel than the others, a vessel to which a good deal of attention had been given and in the production of which great care had been taken in order to embody in her all the best ideas of the time. She cost over half a million dollars, and there can be no question that she is a very excellent ship. She was put on the route this season for the first time. This has not been as difficult a season as some others have been. Still, notwithstanding the mild weather we have had, the ' Earl Grey ' has had to contend with a good deal of very heavy ice. She is a splendid ship and ought to be able to do the work if any vessel that can be constructed at this time could do it. I crossed in her myself in the early part of last month on the way back from Prince Edward Island to Ottawa. There was not much ice in the harbour, but there was much ice off P-oint Prim, on Prince Edward Island, ice so heavy that, as the captain told me, it would have stopped either of the other vessels. But the ' Earl Grey ' was able to make her way through it without difficulty, at the rate of four or five miles an hour. I have mentioned these vessels, not because I am going to discuss very much or at all the class of vessels we required on that route. I think the government have now given us

a vessel as good as they could well give. But, boats are like other things, they cannot perform impossibilities. We have to consider the various routes between Prince Edward Island and the mainland, and here we strike upon a rather vexed question. There are a number of proposed routes between Prince Edward and the mainland, each of which has its advocates who insist upon that particular route as the one best adapted for winter communication. I think it fair to assume that we in Prince Edward Island, to whom this matter of winter communication is a matter of very vital importance, and who are therefore compelled to pay attention to it, are possibly in a better position to form an opinion upon this matter than are those who are not forced to consider it so carefully.
Now, I do not propose to describe the various routes at length, but I may mention them.
Beginning at the western end of the island there is a route that the people of Summerside and Prince county insist on very strongly, that is between Summer-side and Cape Tonnentine. That route has been tried once or twice and the Summer-side people say it has not been sufficiently tried, but so far I do not know that the experiment has been an unqualified success. If that route could be made a success I for one would be quite satisfied to accept it.
Further down you have the route between Cape Traverse and Cape Tormentine, that is the route of the old winter ice boats which we used sometimes to help haul over with a strap. This is also the site of the proposed tunnel; it is the narrowest place between Prince Edward Island and the mainland, the distance from shore to shore being 7i to eight miles. If communication could be kept up there it would seem to be the natural connection between the mainland and Prince Edward Island, because it is so much narrower than the other passages. Very strong objections are, however, raised to it by many people. One is the enormous cost of the piers to be' constructed there, and in addition to that you have on the New Brunswick side reefs running out li or 2J miles from the shore, which it is contended would be very dangerous. On the island side there are also flats running out a long distance. The ice between them is always on the move and the current runs about 4 miles an hour. The contention is that a ship_ might be carried a little out of her way by these currents and touch a reef or flat, which would be the last we would know about that ship.
Further to the east there is a route between Souris or Georgetown and Cape George in Nova Scotia. This route has strong advocates, and if it could be made
permanent and could have continuous communication I do not know that I would raise objection to it. It would be at the extreme end of the island and would necessitate more railway carriage than some of the other routes, but we would look on that as a small matter If the route could be established and continuous Communication maintained. On that route we have a good harbour on the Prince Edward Island side, at Souris. Although it is not very deep it is generally accessible in winter by craft of this nature, and has frequently open water. Georgetown harbour is one of the best harbours to be found anywhere, a magnificent harbour, and no fault could be found with it. But I do not know what could be done at Gape George because, so far as I know, there is no harbour there, or a very inferior one, and it would require a somewhat extensive breakwater to provide an artificial harbour. I am informed by those who say they know that there is always open water there at the change of the tides, and I presume they are correct. I shall not express an opinion of that route because I have not been able to get as much information about it as I have about some of the others.
Then we have the two routes to which I wish especially to call attention. We have the route which has been used for the last third of a century between Georgetown in Prince Edward Island, and Pictou in Nova Scotia. Georgetown, as I have already said, is an exceedingly good port, we have little or no fault to find with it. It has deep water and is very accessible. But when we come to Pictou we have a different story to tell. In order to understand the objection to Pictou I wish to call attention to the configuration of the Straits of Northumberland. The eastern end of the strait is open to the northeast winds, which blow right into the eastern end of the straits and fill them with ice. There is a space of 250 miles through which that northeast wind blows directly from the Straits of Belle Isle into Pictou harbour, and when that wind is blowing, and it is a prevailing one, it fills the entrance to Pictou harbour full up, it packs it from side to side, and the ice grounds and is packed from top to bottom. It makes a solid and impervious mass through which no ship ever built or ever to be built can force a passage. That state of affairs^ has continued for a greater or less length of time during different seasons. The longest time I remember was five years ago when one of the winter steamers was shut inside of Pictou harbour for 59 days and the other was shut out of Pictou harbour for 59 days. But while that was the longest it was not the only instance of vessels being unable to make Pictou harbour. I happened to be over there myself in that

particular season, and the ice was so jammed and grounded on the bottom that even the tides were affected by it. No ship that could be built can go through ice if it cannot dispose of the ice as it breaks it. You can put a ship into heavy ice if it is floating and she can break it if there is sea room to let the broken floes of ice be disposed of, or in some sorts of ice if the boat can pass the ice under her, although that, of course, requires plenty of depth. You cannot do that when the ice is jammed between two coasts and grounded on the bottom, and that is the case in Pictou.
I wish to call attention to one or two extracts which I gave last year upon this subject, but which I think are of sufficient importance to be repeated. Owing to the difficulties we had five years ago, surveys and reports were ordered to be made by the Dominion government. Among those who took this matter up under the instructions of the government was Mr. Shewan, the resident engineer of the Department of Public Works in St. John, New Brunswick, who. in his report speaks as follows:
Up to this time the winter steamer lias been crossing from Pictou to Georgetown, a distance of about 42 miles, with more or less irregularity occasioned by the ice.
He speaks of more or less irregularity and refers to the ice being driven into the eastern end of the straits by the northeast wind. I am anxious to emphasize this fact that the ice which causes our troubles, with which we have to contend, which the government steamers have to fight against and which the government have to deal with in trying to keep up continuous communication with the mainland, is not ice produced there, that ice does not originate in the straits or Pictou harbour, but to the north up towards Belle Isle and in the sea between Belle Isle and Pictou. It is brought down by the wind and is driven in as I say.
When the ice is packed as in this manner, it is almost impossible for a steamer to force her way through, as will be seen from the following from Admiral Makaroff's description of the voyage of the ' Ermack/ who found it easier to break the ice in the Polar seas with that vessel than in the Baltic, because in the Arctic seas the ice is broken, which in the Baltic is extended from land to land.
That is exactly a parallel case with what happened at the harbour of Pictou. As a matter of fact, Pictou with a northeast wind is simply an ice pocket or rather an ice bottle, in which there is a very tight cork, and I doubt very much if even a corkscrew could go through that cork. Admiral Makaroff, in describing the voyage of the ' Ermack ' says:
Floes of ice might he several miles or several fathoms in length. Between the ice Mr. WARBTiRTON,
floes are the lanes, which are very irregular. Sometimes the ice-floes are pressed against each other and sometimes not. When the ice is not pressed, the progress of -the ship is very easy. Floes of ice even nine miles long move away and give passage to the ship. But the fact is that even ice 14 feet thick cracks when charged by the ship, provided there is room to remove the broken parts.
There is where the whole question comes in. You must have room for the removal of the broken parts. A report was also made by Mr. Gobeil, formely deputy minister of Public Works. In the course of his report he says:
From an inspection of the chares it appears that the line from Pictou to Georgetown is where, probably, the ice masses in the greater quantity, and from the direction of the currents, is likely to remain a longer time to prevent the passage of the ferry steamer.
He adds, and this covers a great part of the opposition that may be offered to the change of route:
Of course there is a disposition always to accept whatever is as immutable, and in changing the establishment of anything that has become, w-orthily or unworthily, by lapse of time an institution, local prejudices will be met.
This will prove the great difficulty now, as, not unnaturally, there will always be opposition to a change, by the port or ports to and from which the service is now carried. This should not affect the question.
I think that the remark of Mr. Gobeil will be accepted as correct, that a matter of that kind should not affect the situation. If the service cannot successfully and continuously be performed on the route where it has been during the last 34 or 35 years from Georgetown, surely it is time to make a change and see if we cannot find a route somewhere else. In regard to Pictou I will also read from a report made by Mr. F. W. Hyndman, who was formerly an employee of the British government and who was a first-class hydrographer. He says:
In order that my remarks may he intelligently understood, it is necessary that you have two charts before you, one of the St. Lawrence and another of Prince Edward Island and the Straits of Northumberland. Both these charts are published by the Hydrographic Office, London, and can be had for a small sum at some of onr stores in this city.
If yon will glance at the chart of the Gulf of St. Lawrence and get your eye on Pictou, you will see at once that it is open to the northeasterly winds right up to the Straits of Belle Isle, a distance of some 250 miles. Those winds largely prevail in the winter and the consequence is that Pictou is merely a pocket for che drift and rafting ice of the gulf. Only two years ago

That is five years ago.

-this was shown by both winter steamers on this route being tied up for fifty-nine consecutive days, leaving no means of transporting freight, and forcing passengers and mails to be carried across the straits at Cape Traverse in open boats, a distance of 8 to 10 miles, with much risk and great discomfort on all occasions, and no improvement on the means in use a full century ago.
I referred to one of the stoppages which have taken place there. In the winter of 1898 I was stuck at Pictou ten days and was kept there by a northeast wind which blocked the place with ice. Many other stoppages have taken place. I looked up the other day in the reports of the department to see the record of a few more of these stoppages and I found that in 1898:
The steamer entered upon the winter mail service on the 25th December. It was not considered prudent to continue the ' Stanley ' on the Charlottetown and Pictou route; the steamer therefore kept up communication between Georgetown and Pictou until the 22nd of January, 1898, when the ship was hemmed in by heavy packed ice off Pictou island; in trying to get through between Pictou island and the ice jam the ship ran aground on the reef. After emptying the after-ballast tank the steamer was backed off without damage on the 23rd of January. The ice loosening up, the steamer returned to Georgetown, finding it impossible to get into Pictou. On the 24th January the steamer left for Pictou again, but could not get in. The passengers and mails were landed by ice boats. The mails were transferred to the Capes route on the 26th January. The steamer was jammed in the ice at Pictou from the 27th of January to the 2nd of February.
Again in 1901:
The _ winter service between Charlottetown and Pictou began on January 7, the ' Stanley ' running in conjunction with the steamer * 11 in to,' each boat making bi-weekly trios. On February 5, the ' Stanley ' got caught in the ice off Pictou harbour and remained in the ice until February 20, and did not arrive at Georgetown until February 21.
Again, the same year:
Owing to the heavy ice in the harbour of Pictou between February 5 and 21, and also on account of the shoal water on the bar the steamer was unable to move out of Pictou harbour until February 19. This matter was made more serious by the fact that the steamer ' Stanley ' was at the same time icebound six miles out of Pictou harbour.
Again, in 1902:
The service between the two latter places was begun on January 10. The service was fairly regular until February 12, when the ' Minto ' was caught in heavy" ice off the end of Pictou island and remained fast until February 15. She was then able to get into Georgetown.
In 1905:
In leaving Georgetown on January 25, 1905, the ice was found to be very heavy and the * 101
' Stanley ' returned to Georgetown, and although repeated attempts were made to force the steamer through the ice, it was found impossible to cross to Pictou until March 3, when the ' Stanley ' forced her way to the Pictou ice barrier, and the passengers and mails were transferred over the barrier to the steamer ' Minto ' two miles way. The ' Stanley ' then returned to Georgetown. It was found impossible to make another crossing until March 16, when the ice barrier, off Pictou, was reached and the cargo transferred to the ' Minto.' On March 21, the ' Stanley ' reached Pictou harbour.
I know about that because I was there.
On February 25, 1907, on a trip from Georgetown the ' Minto ' was caught by a heavy ice-jam, in a strong gale and thick snow storm, and did not reach Pictou until March 2, and from that date until March 19 it was found impossible to reach Georgetown again, although several^ attempts were made. The return trip to Pictou was accomplished only on March 26.
Last year was a very good year, but even last year passengers left Georgetown on Monday and got back to Georgetown on the following Saturday. Several other cases occurred in which passengers were prevented for several days from getting across. I have gone into some detail with reference to this question because I wished to emphasize the fact, which I mentioned in my opening remarks, that our difficulties are due not to ice that is made in the straits but to ice that is driven down and fills up the harbour and straits. It is practically polar ice that is driven in there. That ice does not go through the straits. It is held up, to some extent, by Pictou island, and to some extent, by Cape Bear. Some of it passes these two points and is held up at Point Prim which is a long narrow point running out three or four miles from the Prince Edward Island shore. This polar ice does not get beyond that. In Charlottetown we have often complained, and complained without reason, of the steamer not getting backwards and forwards. We knew the condition of the ice in Charlottetown harbour and between Charlottetown and the mainland to be all right, but we could not see over Point Prim to discover what was there. We invariably found that the difficulty lay east of Point Prim where the ice was massed. You cannot judge of the conditions upon the state of the weather there. If you know the direction of the wind you may form an opinion. If it is northeast you may make up your mind that there is going to be trouble. After giving the George-town-Pictou route a trial for over a third of a century, and having proved successfully and absolutely that it is impossible to keep up winter communication by that route I do say that it is fair, it is right and that it is reasonable to



ask that some other route should be tried to find whether there is a possibility of keeping up that communication.
We believe, after years of experience, that we have the most simple and direct route between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. Efforts have been made to show that Charlottetown harbour is blocked up in the same manner as Pictou during the winter months, but that is absolutely incorrect, and the fact is that the channel route into Charlottetown harbour was never known to be blocked with ice. There are, of course, flats on both sides of Charlottetown harbour and points running out upon which the ice grounds and stays, but we never purposed running steamers over these flats or over these points. Our purpose is to navigate the deep and splendid channel between these points. I may say that the question of the ice in Charlottetown harbour has been investigated time and time again. Even since I brought the matter up in the House last session there are those who have insisted that the channel leading into Charlottetown is too narrow to make in winter. I have here a copy of the admiralty chart and it shows that -where the main channel debouches from the deep water of Northumberland straits towards Charlottetown some three or four miles out the entrance to the channel between the eighteen-foot marks-on these admiralty charts-I believe they give the low water so that the figures I shall read are taken between the eighteen-foot marks

this shows that the entrance to the harbour on the outside is three and one quarter miles in width.
