maintopic: WINTER COMMUNICATION WITH PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND.
speechtext:
When the House rose at six o'clock I was making some reference to the harbour conditions of Charlottetown during the winter season, and I proposed to make some references to the admiralty chart of the harbour, a portion of which, covering the entrance to the harbour, I have had copied. I may say that the soundings of which I propose to give the figures, were taken at the lowest spring tide, the lowest water to be found, according to the custom of the admiralty, so that the soundings will be accurate and safe, and a vessel cannot be misled in accepting them. At the extreme outer end of the channel extending from the harbour, where it breaks away from the deeper water of the straits, the measurement between the 18-foot lines-the two lines on opposite sides of the channel, where the minimum depth is 18 feet-the width across the channel is three and one-quarter miles. We are some-Mr. WARBURTON.
times told that the entrance to Charlottetown harbour is so narrow that a vessel cannot make it in the winter time, or, some people say, at any other time, without special aids to navigation. Across the channel at that point the depth of water varies from the minimum of 18 feet on the one side to 21 feet, 34 feet, 34 feet again, 35 feet, 31 feet, and back to 18 feet on the other side. About two miles farther in other measurements were taken. There the channel passes between the island of St. Peter and Governor's island, which lie on either side of the entrance, but at some distance from it. From these islands shoal water runs out for a considerable distance; but there the width of the channel between the 18 feet lines is one and three-quarter miles; and any sailor who cannot make his way through a channel of that width ought not to be let off dry land. At that point the depth varies from 18 feet on one side to 26 feet, 34 feet, 32 feet, 28 feet, and back to 18 feet on the other side. Towards one side of the channel at that point there is the Fitzroy rock about which some trouble has been made. Some have said that it is impossible to navigate the channel with that rock there. It is not a very large rock, and I find that the lowest water over it is 20 feet at low spring tide, and the depth varies from that to 21 feet, 27 feet, 28 feet, 25 feet, 22 feet which shows that vessels could sail over it with perfect safety. At about three miles from that point the channel suddenly narrows off from the reef that runs about three miles from St. Peter's island and another from the mainland of Prince Edward Island, but even there it is three-quarters of a mile wide, and the depth of water is 72 feet. At a distance of another mile and a half the channel becomes one-third of a mile wide and there the depth of water is 57 or 58 feet. That width continues right to the mouth of the harbour between the Blockhouse light and the land on the other side. There, between the two points forming the entrance, which is the narrowest part, the channel is one-third of a mile wide, and between these two points there is deep [DOT]water almost up to the shore, so that it would be almost impossible for any man to get out of his course there. At that point the water is 73 feet deep. From there the channel continues for a couple of miles to the basin of Charlottetown harbour on a straight line according to the range lights; and in it the depth of water varies from 73 feet to 77 feet. About half way to the wharf there is a short bend to the right, and then a straight line to the wharf. From the point where this change is made the channel continues of a uniform width of about one-third of a mile. Inside there is a large harbour of deep-water varying from 61 feet to 44 feet, and the wharf will

accommodate a vessel drawing 26 feet of water, while 100 yards from the wharf there is a depth of 58 feet. It is said that this channel gets filled with ice. To begin with, there is no wind that can drive ice into that harbour. We who have spent our lives at Charlottetown know that; but people who desire to deflect the vessel from her present course there try to make out that ice drives into the channel. The mere fact that the channel has a depth of 70 feet and has two inward and two outward tides every day, with a tremendous current which would prevent the ice getting very thick, is sufficient to convince any man that that channel could not get blocked with ice. At the narrow entrance at the Blockhouse light there is no difficulty, because the only ice to be encountered there is harbour ice, which is never more than from 18 inches to 2 feet thick, and the ' Earl Grey ' will go through that at the rate of from six to eight miles an hour. The ' Minto ' or the ' Stanley ' going through such ice was a sight worth seeing, but this much more powerful ship goes through it at much greater speed.
We have taken the precaution for many years to have this thing tested, because I do not pretend to come before this House without being able to put the facts before you, which we have proved to be true. The board of trade in Charlottetown took measures to test this for a number of years, and they employed Captain John Gillies, an old experienced sea captain who has been residing in Charlottetown for a great many years, to make observations of the harbour ice, and of the channel ice, particularly of the channel ice leading into the harbour. I will Tead from a part of his report:
I have been asked by Mr. L. B. Miller, secretary of the board of trade here, to give a condensed report of the conditions, of the ice in the Hillsboro' bay and Charlottetown harbour during the three years (winters) 1904-5-0" that I was engaged to make actual surveys of the same.
In each of the aforementioned years the surveys were made during the month of March, when it was considered the most ice would be found, and the hardest task to make the harbour.
I would call attention to the fact that that year was the year in which steamers could not get in and out of Pictou for 59 days.
From the reports submitted at various times the ice varied in thickness from 28 inches to 18, and the average ice in ' the ship's course ' was 24 inches, covering from 7 to 9 fathoms of water.
While it is true the ' Minto ' tried to make Charlottetown in March 1905, and got stuck off St. Peter's Island bar in a reported thickness of 15 feet of ice, it is equally true that I was almost immediately sent to make a survey and found, by actual measurement, there 101 i
was only 5 feet where she stuck. I can account for the discrepancy in one way only: In my case the ice was measured, and in the other case it must have been judged from the bridge of the ship. Only one week after my survey was made and reported the ' Minto ' made another attempt to reach Charlottetown and was successful.
In making the aforesaid survey, I found where the * Minto ' had stuck, there being 5 feet of ice and 9 fathoms of water. I then measured 40 yards from -this spot toward St. Peter's island and I found 2 feet of ice with 7 fathoms of water, and 60 yards nearer the island I got the same thickness of ice with 5 fathoms of water, while at the block-house (entrance to the harbour) there was but 18 inches of ice.
This is a point I wish to emphasize, bei-cause that is the point made by those who are opposed to this route:
As the ice does not raft in this bay to any appreciable extent owing to the board ice and the prevailing northeast winds, it is my belief that with better aids to navigation there should be but little difficulty in making this a winter port, there being plenty of sea-room and water, and ships will have to centend with no running ice.
Again last year, although it was a mild winter, we had difficulty getting into Pictou harbour. There was no ice-breaker. The ' Earl Grey ' was not ready, and this work was done by the old vessel. In isome cases last year passengers got on board at) Georgetown on Monday and were out all the week trying to get to Pictou and back to Georgetown on Saturday, without having reached their destination. The last time that occurred, passengers were delayed from three to five days, though the winter was a favourable one; there was not one, day last winter in which those steamers could not have got in and out of Charlottetown harbour. Now, last year,-and I suppose it was done at my request-and in view of the fact that I had brought this matter up in the House, observations were ordered to be made, and the board of trade sent two master mariners to investigate, Captain John Gillies, whose earlier report I have already Tead, and Captain C. E. Myers, who has been living in Charlotte-) town for the last 15 or 20 years. On March1 16 they made a report to the board of trade, of which the following is an extract:
Having been commissioned by you in your capacity as president of the board of trade, to secure data of the conditions of the ice between this harbour and Point Prim, we beg to report as follows:-
We began our survey of the ice in the harbour this morning, and found open water from Murphy's point (red buoy) to Trout point at harbour's mouth. At the latter place, in range with Brighton light ranges (ship's course), we found open water 12 fathoms deep. From that point we proceeded due south 100 yards with only 4 inches of

ice continuing on same course another 100 yards we found G inches of ice with 12 fathoms of water. We kept on the same course for 150 yards and found 8 inches of ice alongside a vein of open water in channel. We then made a circuit around the open water a dis-ance of about 150 yards, estimated-the ice being too dangerous to carry us for actual measurement-and came in line with the range lights and again found 6 inches of ice with 11 fathoms of water. Proceeding 200 yards on the ranges (about south) we got 4 inches of ice and 10 fathoms of water. Continuing on ship's course seaward 200 yards we measured 5 inches of ice and sounded 11 fathoms of water. On the same course and distance we found 4 inches of ice and unsafe to take soundings. Ice from this point unsafe to continue in channel to St. Peter's Island bar, consequently we left the centre of the channel and proceeded to the east edge of same until we came to 6 fathoms of water and found 4 inches of ice. We continued on south by west in order to get into deeper water for a distance of 400 yards. Here the ice was parted in line with Lowther's point, south shore, and Pownal Head.
Those are two points 8 or 10 miles outside the harbour.
Beyond this it was unsafe to proceed any further for the ice was only 2 inches thick.
We found open water from the black buoy extending seaward past St. Peter's Island bar, Point Prim, and as far seaward as we could see with glasses.
From our survey we are in a position to state there is no ice from Point Prim to Charlottetown to hinder a steamer making this port. In fact, following the ship s course from the three tides out the ice mentioned in the foregoing report was of such a nature as not to present a serious obstacle to many of our summer boats.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it does appear to me that these facts ought to satisfy any reasonable person that Charlottetown harbour is quite accessible during the winter season. I wish also to say something about the harbour across the straits at Tatamagouche, or Brule. But first let me speak of the work that has been done this season. The ' Earl Grey ' and the ' Minto ' were put upon the route between Charlottetown and Pictou. The ' Minto ' made the trip and changed to Georgetown. The captain of the ' Minto could not be induced to get away from Charlottetown, but the captain of the ' Earl Grey ' kept on the route-I crossed over with him myself. The ship passed backwards and forwards from Pictou, making the trip one way each day; she used to make the trip in three or four hours, and the last day in five hours. There was no difficulty whatever. On one occasion, on the 17th of January the Earl Grey' left Charlottetown intending to return. The harbour ice presented no difficulties, but when she got round Point Prim she struck, some miles down the straits, the Polar*ice which had Mr. WARBURTON.
filled up the eastern end of the straits. The Polar ice does not drift past Point Prim. Point Prim is the farthest western point where that ice reaches. So once you arq west of Point Prim you are sure to have water and ice conditions through which the vessel can go without much difficulty. But this time when the vessel was going to Pictou she got into this heavy ice and was stopped three times. She kept on to Pictou, and the captain was afraid to risk the new vessel without instructions, and decided to go to Georgetown next day. But he made that trio to Pictou notwithstanding the fact that he met this heavy ice east of Point Prim, and where he had to stop the boat and butt the ice three times. He had to go round the eastern entrance to Pictou, which lengthened the route to over 60 miles, and he did it in five hours. Captain Brown, the captain of the vessel, was empowered to make the effort again.
I thought this matter of sufficient importance to Prince Edward Island for me to get such information with regard to it as I could, so I telegraphed and wrote to the secretary of the Board of Trade and to this same Captain Myers, who wrote the report a few years ago, asking particulars of the cause of the 'Earl Grey' being transferred to Pictou, when, I understood, the entrance to Charlottetown harbour, the harbour itself and the straits outside the harbour were in the best condition for the steamer to get through. The report I had here, indirectly, as I mentioned, was that the vessel had met with heavy ice. However, I thought it better to be definite. So, I wrote to Mr. Miller, the secretary of the Board of Trade. I now quote his reply so far as it relates to this matter:
I have taken, considerable pains to ascertain the facts in connection with the sudden change in going to Georgetown and find the captain acted solely on his own judgment. When he left Charlottetown he intended returning, but when he got round Point Prim and down towards Wood Islands he met such heavy ice that even the ' Earl Grey ' had. to make three smashes to penetrate it. As it was a very cold day and the ice was making fast, the captain concluded it would be best to go to Georgetown. Under the circumstances, I do not think any person could blame him.
I agree with that.
To-day he is back again in Charlottetown, and may be depended upon to give this port a fair trial.
He came back to Charlottetown on the 25th having been away a week. And, from that time until now, he has been making his regular trip. And the ' Minto has joined in the service and both are making the trip. And they will be able to make the trip so long as there is no continuance of northeast winds. We are liable to have an

east wind, which will fill up the eastern end of the straits and Pictou harbour, so that the vessels will again be unable to make their course. Captain Myers, the man who made the report and survey a few years ago, gives me as^the reason the following :
The boat made the time to Pictou (from Charlottetown) in five hours, very good time for mid-winter, but she had to go round Pictou island at least fifteen miles further, >the reason was that the ice was packed in Carribou channel, and between the Indian Rocks and Carribou the ice stopped the boat three times and was very much rafted together. She left here (Charlottetown) and never stopped until after she rounded Point Prim. The trouble all lies between Carribou channel on account of the scarcity of water and the ice around Indian Rocks, that lies straight across the straits. The boat could cross from here to Cape John any day since she had to leave here.
It seems to me that the reports of men who know what they are talking about, thoroughly sound and accomplished men, ought to carry weight and convince every reasonable man as to how matters stand in this regard. Before leaving Charlottetown harbour again, I wish to point out that, in order to make Charlottetown harbour, a perfect winter port, some effective aids of navigation must be provided. When the ice comes in the autumn, the buoys are taken up, so, when the ships come into the harbour, they have to depend entirely upon the lights. Again, in winter, especially when there is ice, there is at times a haze rising from the water, and this haze prevents the men on board the steamers from seeing the lights which are four or five miles away. What is needed in order to make the harbour accessible in any weather is a lighthouse on St. Peter's island bar outside of Charlottetown. This bar runs out from St. Peter's island, and is a sandstone bar, and at low tide there is a depth of five or six feet of water on it. There should be a light there and also a steam whistle. Once the vessel picked up the whistle or the light it would have no difficulty in getting into Charlottetown, because these aids to navigation will overcome the trouble arising from the haze. Of course, there is no difficulty at all so long as the weather is fair. These important aids to navigation are not required solely in the interests of the winter service; they have been looked for by shipowners and others for some time. I have here a copy of a memorial presented to the Charlottetown Board of Trade on this point. It is as follows:
Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island,
February 9, 1909. To the President and Council,
Charlottetown Board of Trade,
Gentlemen,-The undersigned master mariners and owners of sailing vessels sailing to
and from the port of Charlottetown respectfully request your board to use its influence in having a lighthouse with a steam whistle attached-erected on the end of the bar extending from the east end of St. Peter's island-outside Charlottetown.
Now that very large steamers sometimes visit our port, this light has become a necessity, and if built with a steam whistle attached," vessels could make the harbour without difficulty, whereas at present, especially after the buoys are lifted, Charlottetown is an extremely difficult place to make, owing to this long bar.
Charlottetown has one of the finest harbours in the lower provinces, and is a superior and safe port for shelter. With the requested aid to navigation installed-lighthouse and steam whistle-it would not only facilitate ordinary trade, but would be of inestimable benefit to the shipping interests in stormy weather.
This is signed by a number of vessel owners and agents of steamship lines. I think this is sufficient with regard to Charlottetown harbour. The most likely harbour on the mainland coast would be situated in Tatamagouche bay. I cannot say whether it would be best to place it inside Cape John on Tatamagouche bay or the peninsula sometimes called West Brule point; or it might be on the Tatamagouche side. My opinion is that in one of these sections you will find plenty of water on which to make a pier. After last session, being very much interested in this matter, I went over with some others to look at the bay. We sounded off Peninsular point at half tide and found 27 feet of water. Also we found deep water on the Cape John side and on the other side. When we spoke of this matter last year, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) said that he would take measures to have a survey made. He carried out his promise, and men have been there surveying the county to ascertain where the pier could best be built. To carry out the idea would require a pier and a short spur of railway.' The Oxford branch of the Intercolonial is within half a mile of the Tatamagouche -side and within three miles of the Cape John side. The pier would be, perhaps, 900 feet long. I do not think it would be more; 900 feet is what I estimated roughly. Again, if the line of railway were built through to Truro-and it has been mooted for some time and it will certainly be built-it would afford the most direct line, at a distance^ of from 30 to 32 miles, for a connection with the main line at Truro and with the Dominion Atlantic railway, giving the shortest route by 100 miles or more between Prince Edward Island and Boston and other eastern ports of the United States. If the government were to undertake the building of that line, it would seem the businesslike thing. to do. But there is strong reason to believe that, if the government do not want to build it, the Dominion

Atlantic would be ready to do so. I believe that the Nova Scotia government would be ready to give a bonus of $5,000 a mile, and I am under the impression that the Dominion, government would pay $3,200 a mile.^ There would be no difficulty in building the road, and there can be no question that, when running, it would increase the Dominion Atlantic receipts very much. The only question is whether it would not be wiser, as it is close to the Intercolonial and will connect at Truro, for the government to build a branch if it is to be built. However, that is a matter for them to decide, on which I do not propose to offer an opinion. Then at the mouth of Tatamagouche bay, almost exactly in the [DOT]centre of a line crossing the mouth, is Am-let island, on which there is a lighthouse now. It is a small island, not much larger than these buildings. That lighthouse ought to be equipped with a steam whistle, and that I think would be all the additional aid required on that side. The more inquiry there is made about the Tatamagouche bay site, the more satisfied people must become that it is an ideal winter port. No wind that blows can block it; it is near the centre of the strait where the tide meets so that there is little fluctuation and the current is only about half a mile an hour; it is protected on the east by Pictou island, and by Cape Bear on the Prince Edward shore. On the north it is protected by Prince Edward Island itself. The western ice never gets up to the middle of the straits, it blocks at the western end. The western end of Prince Edward Island looks like part of the mainland; in fact, when Jacques Cartier discovered the island he sailed around there and not finding a harbour sailed back, he did not see where the entrance to the straits was, and did not know he had discovered an island. Then the western ice is never as heavy as the ice from the east that causes the difficulty at other places. Last year at the board of trade of the maritime provinces this matter was taken up, and after 'thorough discussion the following resolution was passed:
Whereas, the terms of union made and entered into between Canada and the province of Prince Edward Island in the year 1873, provided for continuous steam communication winter and summer, between the said province and the mainland.
And whereas, the routes hitherto in use by the winter steamers have failed to fulfil that condition-resulting in serious loss and inconvenience to the people of the province, and considerable loss to the Dominion by way of compensation for said non-fulfilment of" the terms of union.
This board of trade of the maritime provinces desires to express its opinion that in justice to the province, as well as to the whole Dominion, an attempt should now be made by the new winter steamer ' Earl Grey ' to solve the question of continuous winter steam com-Mr. WAKBITRTON.
munication, and recommend to that end that a complete survey of the approaches and possible pier sites in the Bay of Tatamagouche be made by the Dominion government without delay; and that if found feasible and practicable that route should be adopted hereafter, being considerably shorter in distance, and very much less liable to be packed with gulf ice than Pictou harbour, as found by actual and long experience of over thirty-six years.
That survey has been made and for that report among other papers, I am moving.
The officials of the Department of Marine and Fisheries have taken considerable trouble in this matter; they sent their representative down to make a thorough and accurate survey of this section. His instructions were to survey only inside of Cape John, but I suggested to the department that while they were about it they should survey all around and I believe that was done.
In speaking of the summer route I shall not refer to the steamship service at the western end, between Summerside and Point du Chene. They provided an excellent service and I do not know that any one has found fault with it. The Steam Navigation Company of Prince Edward Island have two fine steamers running between Charlottetown and Pictou and Summerside and Point du Chene. But like many people who have been for thirty or forty or fifty years in one groove, it is hard to get them out of that groove. Forty-five or fifty years ago the summer steamer was run between Charlottetown and Brule in Tatamagouche bay, but when the railway was built to Pictou she transferred from Brule to Pictou to make connection with the railway which of course was the most sensible thing to do at that time. Had the railway been built to Brule af that time, they would not have left Brule, because it is more convenient. The Brule route would shorten the distance materially. As we are now situated in summer it takes three days to get to Halifax and do a day's business and return, unless you leave Halifax at seven o'clock in the morning which is too early to do any business, you cannot get away until the next day, so that it takes three days no matter how short the business may be. Taking the other route it would be practicable to make two round trips a day between Charlottetown and Brule. The distance is twenty-five miles while the distance to Pictou is fifty-four miles, and the distance on land is also somewhat shortened. By the present route from Charlottetown to Pictou and from Pictou to Halifax we have to travel 170 miles. Crossing over to Tatamagouche and going by Brule, you cut sixty miles off that distance, making the trip 110 miles. It will at once be seen what a handicap this distance is. The service is not run to

accommodate our people at all, they have to stop at Pictou and other places and we do not think that this delay is right, fair or necessary. If the route I suggest is adopted for the summer steamers there would be no difficulty, with proper connections, in doing business in Halifax, which ought to be our principal winter port, within a reasonable time. I brought this matter to the attention of the Department of Trade and Commerce and also of this House last session, and pointed these things out to them. They brought the matter to the' attention of the Steam Navigation Company. I pointed out that the reason there was so little trade and passenger communication with Halifax was that the means of communication were so poor that the transportation facilities were so bad and slow that we simply went elsewhere, and I thought it was in the interests of our friends in Halifax and along that line to back us up in getting an improvement made. I put down the smallness of the traffic then at Halifax to that fact of the deficient accommodation, but when the department applied to the Steam Navigation Company the secretary wrote and said it would not do at all as only 3 per cent of their passenger traffic was to Halifax. In other words they gave the reason why they did not do business as a reason why they should not attempt to do business. No business man who is alive and looking after his own interests would make that as an excuse; he might know that the reason he did very little business was that the facili-' ties were not afforded. Give the facilities and the business will be done. That could almost be called a business maxim, improve the transportation and you will improve the trade. The Steam Navigation Company have splendid ships and do good work on their line, but you cannot get them out of their groove. They have a contract to carry the mails and carry them well, they treat you well on board and it is hard to say anything against' them, but I am talking business.
They say there is no reason why they should make two trips a day backward and forward, and they say it is not required all the time. I think it is not required all the time, but it is required part of the time. They say that they have to take in freight and that it is impossible for them to make two trips a day each way. To a certain extent I admit that. There are certain times of the year when they are handling a great quantity of freight and therefore what they say at that time will be perfectly true. At that time we do not want them to make two trips a day. There is no passenger traffic in the spring and fall when the steamers are leaving Charlottetown and Summerside loaded down with freight, but, in the summer months, from June until
the latter part of September, they have very little freight, and they are carrying a very .arge and rapidly increasing number of passengers. The passenger traffic on these boats during the summer months is such that the boats are absolutely over-crowded. The crowd is so great that it is almost impossible to get a seat. The saloons and every place where people can find standing room are crowded, but that does not last the whole season. We do not ask them to make two round trips in the spring and fall when the press of freight traffic is on, but all we ask them to do is to make two trips a day when the big passenger and tourist traffic is on. Not only has the passenger and tourist traffic increased rapidly, but it is bound to go on increasing. Prince Edward Island is becoming rapidly recognized as one of the most desirable summer resorts during the mid-summeT months, the number of tourists last year was greater than ever before, and I expect that the number during the present year will be greater than that of last year. So that, as far as that contention goes, I think there is nothing in it. If, when tenders are next called for the carrying of the mails, and you give the companies the alternative of running between Brule and Charlottetown and between Pictou and Charlottetown, the contention is set up that the companies find it impossible to give a good service between Brule and Charlottetown, I will undertake to say that I will find a company to do it.
I understood from the minister before Christmas that it was the intention to send an inspector to Tatamagouche bay to inspect the ice conditions there during the present winter. I understand that a man is down there and I hope in the not distant future to have his report. I have gone into this matter somewhat exhaustively and at greater length than I had intended to, but I thought when I was about it that I would like to make a clear statement of the_ conditions as far as I was able to do it. I wish to Tefer to a statement I made last year about whiqh I was hauled over the coals at a local election in Prince Edward Island and also in the press. I am not looking for the pound of flesh; I am not one of those who believe in the pound of flesh theory. It has been the custom for Prince Edward Islanders to look for the pound of flesh, or rather, for members who represented the people of Prince Edward Island, or papers who pretended to represent them, to insist upon their pound of flesh. It was not the true voice of Prince Edward Island and I do not propose to speak in that way. I think it is a poor way of going about this business. What I want to do is to take a fair and reasonable view of this matter. I believe that

anything that tends to the improvement of transportation between different ports of the Dominion tends to build up the Dominion, and I like to place anything in the shape of a public work on the principle of the general good of the country, not upon the principle of the pound of flesh, not upon any hard and fast, cut and dried resolution, but on the ground that it is going to be for the general good of Canada. Improvements in transportation between Prince Edward Island and the mainland, while almost vital to us, are of very great importance to the people of the mainland. There is no part of Canada in which the merchants and manufacturers like better to sell their wares than in Prince Edward Island. Prince Edward Islanders have the reputation of being the best payers there are; they are the largest buyers per head and the farmers, taking them man for man, are the best off amongst the farming population of Canada. There are no wealthy men, there are no poor men, but they all buy and use manufactured goods. An enormous quantity of manufactured goods is sold and paid for in Prince Edward Island considering the population of the island. It is upon that ground and upon the ground of union and consolidation that I wish to place this matter before the House. Mr. Speaker, I apologize for taking up so much of your time, but I now close by moving the resolution which stands in my name.
Mr.'E. M. MACDONALD (Pictou). Mr. Speaker, I have not had the pleasure of listening to the long and interesting statement of the case presented by my hon. friend from Queens, Prince Edward Island (Mr. Warburton). Those who are interested in the advocacy of the cause which he presents cannot say that my hon. friend has not brought to bear upon his proposi tion a great deal of industry, a great deal of care and that he has not presented it with some elaboration. I do not propose to follow him through the various phases of the subject as he has discussed it, and there are one or two points only t-o which I would like to refer. My hon. friend has spoken of the fact that the boats of the Prince Edward Island Navigation Company do not give that service to the people of the island which is desired or which he thinks is in their best interests. I have taken occasion in a previous discussion of this question, to point out that the solution of the inconvenience which my hon. friend complains of would be arrived if by these boats, instead of running from Charlottetown to the mainland in the morning and returning at night, would start from the mainland in the morning and return there at night. The result would be, in so far as connection with Nova Scotia is Mr. WARBURTON.
concerned, that not only would the outside world be able to get on this tight little island very much more expeditiously than they now do, but the people there could get away from it and get back whenever they had business to do very .much more satisfactorily than they can under the present arrangement. I am surprised that my hon. friend should once more undertake to entertain the House about this imaginary ice bar that forms in front of the mouth of the Pictou harbour. I was born in the little town of Pictou and have lived there some forty years. Only once in all the years during which communication has been maintained from that place with Prince Edward Island has an ice barrier existed there at the time of winter navigation. Since that accidental circumstance which occurreed some years ago hon. gentlemen in discussing this question have talked about as if it were a permanent and continuous obstruction that came as sure as the winter came. Any hon. gentleman who wants-to make an argument for better facilities for Prince Edward Island, whether by increased facilities or a.change of route, and who rests his argument upon the basis which has no existence in fact and which is an accidental circumstance which should not be used as the basis of any argument for a change in the conditions of affairs. The unfortunate thing for my hon. friend's proposition is that other hon. gentlemen from Prince Edward Island do not agree with him. I have not heard the remarks of the hon. gentlemen who come from the east of the island, but I venture the prediction that they will not agree with my hon. friend from Queens in the proposition that the present winter port should be changed and that a new and experimental route should be established between Charlottetown and Tatamagouche.
There are some things in my hon. friend's proposition which are worthy of consideration, but the. government and the country would naturally expect that before conditions are to be changed there should at least be absolute unanimity on the part of the people who are making the request. At Pictou you have had for years large sums expended on terminal facilities. We have had facilities existent there for almost half a century, and an established trade, and before all that is abandoned there must be some good reason given for a large expenditure elsewhere. When the hon. gentleman talks about Tatamagouche and Brule, those of us who live on the mainland, whose judgment is formed not by theory or on the strength of the accidental visit of a gentleman who goes over on a junketing excursion in the summer time know that it would cost $1,000,000 to the people of this country to provide at Tatamagouche and Brule the facilities that

the hon. gentleman speaks of. The dredging that would have to be done to enable you to reach either of these points, outside of every other consideration, would be so vast that hon. gentlemen on the other side who sometimes think that the Minister of Public Works is very enterprising, would stand aghast at it. There is only one possibly feasible point on the mainland in Tatamagouche bay, with deep water and possible conditions, and that is Cape John. If my hon. friend (Mr. Warburton) can induce the good people of Prince Edward Island, who are interested in this matter, to press for communication there in the summer time at least, before we make experiments in the winter, I would be glad to aid in anything that can be done in furthering a favourable consideration of that proposition. But, the proposition as advanced by my hon. friend (Mr. Warburton) is one that should be approached with the greatest possible care. Communication between Charlottetown and Cape John is the only phase of the proposition made by my hon. friend '(Mr. Warburton) that is worthy of consideration or investigation, and that may be feasible. But there are difficulties in the way; difficulties with regard to expenditure and with regard to changing existing conditions, and these would have to be considered. The proposition to go to Tatamagouche bay or Brule cannot be considered as a reasonable proposition. I would like my hon. friend (Mr. Warburton) to get the people of Prince Edward Island to agree on his proposition before he attempts to dangle it before the eyes of the people of Nova Scotia. We on the mainland have practical knowledge of the conditions, and1 we would like to see some unanimity and consensus of opinion with regard to these suggestions in order that they may be fully and fairly considered, and in order that the country might look upon them as worthy of consideration.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. W. MADDIN (Cape Breton South).
maintopic: WINTER COMMUNICATION WITH PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I draw the attention of the House to the fact that as an inducement to Prince Edward Island to enter confederation, the parliament of Canada promised the people of that province continuous communication between the island and the mainland. For over 40 years the harbour of Pictou has been used as a port of entry from Prince Edward Island, but I would point out that Pictou harbour is open to the northeasterly gales which prevail during the spring months and is but a pocket for the drift ice which is carried from Hudson bay and the Arctic into the Northumberland straits. For the last 36 or 37 years the port of Pictou has been tried and found wanting. It was promised to the people of Prince Edward Island that under this administration the communication would be made at Brule or Tatamagouche
bay, the distance from which across the Straits of Northumberland is less than the distance by the present Pictou route. It must also be remembered that the tide flow at Brule is considerably less, and that the drift ice cannot form as it does at Pictou harbour. As was pointed out by my hon. friend (Mr. Warburton) such i.s the formation of drift ice in Pictou harbour that in the winter of 1905 communication with the island was cut off for a period of 59 days. It is not alone the concern of the people of Prince Edward Island that there should be continuous communication by steam navigation throughout the year, because the people of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick are also interested. Prince Edward Island can produce all the meats and vegetables that are necessary to supply us, and we should naturally get our supplies from the island, but on account of the uncertainty of communication we are obliged to buy from Ontario during a large part of the year. But the supply is not continuous, the people of Nova Scotia are obliged to buy from the people of Ontario. There is no assurance that purchases made in Charlottetown or in Sydney for delivery during the winter months will be delivered, there being no continuous communication between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. I wish to point out that the harbour of Pictou lies directly exposed to the gales of the northeast and to the flow of ice from the straits of Belle Isle, which retard the spring. This ice field, becoming embanked behind the island of Pictou, and in the Strait of Northumberland behind the island of Prince Edward, lies in such a way that the prevailing temperatures congeal it into hard ice; and I regret that the hon. member who moved this resolution did not press the question on the government as to how often the boat leaving Pictou was obliged to exchange its passengers with the boat leaving the island by reason of the formation of ice between the two. If the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Stanfield) were present he would be able to point out to this House that so favourable was the Liberal government of Nova Scotia to the purport of this resolution that in the elections of 1906 such members of that government and supporters of it as the Hon., now Mr. Justice, Lawrence, and the Hon. B. F. Pearson, pledged themselves to insist upon the permanent route between Prince Edward Island and the mainland being by Brule or the harbour of Tatamagouche, or they would resign their seats. They said that a line of railway constructed from Tatamagouche bay to the town of Truro would save passengers from the island to the mainland at least twelve hours. In view of the fact that the currents in Northumberland strait move in an easterly direction, and the fact that the dist-

ance between Georgetown and Brule, although greater in miles, is in such a geographical position as to exclude the diift ice which comes down from the Strait of Belle Isle, it is up to this government to make an effort towards keeping their pledge by installing a steamer between Prince Edward Island and Brule. At the time the province of British Columbia came into confederation the parliament of Canada promised it continuous communication by rail between the Atlantic and the Pacific. At that time there were only
11,000	people living westward of the Rocky mountains, yet the government of that time, under the late Sir John A. Macdonald, with Sir Charles Tupper as Minister of Railways, did not hesitate to make good their pledge to the people of British Columbia by securing the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway. Efforts were made from time to time by the late Conservative administration to connect Prince Edward Island with the mainland. It was hoped that this might be done by means of an ice-breaking steamship. The 'Stanley' was introduced. She has been tried and found wanting. Since that effort, which was a progressive effort on the part of the Liberal-Conservative administration, great innovations have taken place. It remains for this government either to grant a tunnel to the people of Prince Edward Island or to change the route for steamship travel from Pictou to another and more favourable route, which will maintain continuous steam communication between the island and the other provinces of the Dominion. In the province of Nova Scotia there are many consumers of such products as are produced on the island of Prince Edward. There are people who bring to Nova Scotia during the summer months, Prince Edward Island beef, eggs, butter and other farm products. These people would be glad to continue their patronage to the island during all the twelve months of the year; but this bar of non-continuous communication with the mainland prevents them doing so. If this resolution were given effect to, and if Tatamagouche bay instead of the harbour of Pictou were made the point of arrival, with a branch line of railway to the town of Truro, the people of Nova Scotia would consume, during the winter months, Prince Edward Island beef instead of Ontario beef, as they do now, and Prince Edward Island would be placed in a position that would enable it to compete with the western provinces of Canada all the year round.

I desire to add a few words to the discussion of this very important question. It may not appear very important to other parts of Canada, but to the pro-Mr. MADDIN.
vince I have the honour to represent, with my colleagues, it is a vital one. The transportation question for our farmers has been for many years a burning question, and I congratulate my hon. friend and colleague from Queens, P.E.I., (Mr. War-burton), on the diligence with which he has collected data, and the ability with which he has presented it to this House to-day. I was a little surprised to hear the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) say that after having lived in Pictou for so many years he had never seen barrier ice there but once in his life. Well, Sir, I can say for my part that I have waited outside Pictou harbour for a week or several days at a time, without being able to land. On one occasion the steamer was held in the ice outside Pictou harbour for fifty-nine consecutive days, and at that time it was estimated that the farmers of Prince Edward Island lost over $200,000 on their potatoes alone. They had large quantities of potatoes which they were obliged to leave in their cellars to rot; they could not ship them on account of the steamer being tied up by the ice. I admit that this government has made some honest efforts to improve our transportation facilities. But there is one thing that this government and no other government can do, and that is to change the conditions of the harbour ice. Of course I do not blame the hon. member for Pictou for defending his local harbour. I do not know of any representative in this House that works harder for his constituency than does that hon. gentleman. Sometimes we have to run up against him, because we think that he works a little too hard for the interests of Pictou and incidentally against those of Prince Edward Island. I am sorry the hon, gentleman is not present at this moment, because I do not want to say anything about him in his absence that I would not say in his presence. I was hoping that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries would see his way clear this winter to have left the 'Stanley' there, so that a thorough test could be made of this new route, and that the government could have all the information they need as to the feasibility of this route. No doubt it would be a great advantage to the people of Prince Edward Island if this new route were adopted, because it would do away with the three short hauls which are now an obstacle to transportation. The freight costs almost three times as much as it does from Montreal. Let me give the House a few figures. From Montreal to St. John it costs ten and a half cents per 100 pounds for 735 miles. From Montreal to Halifax ten and a half cents per 100 pounds for 832 miles. From Montreal to Sydney sixteen and a half cents per 100 pounds for 977 miles. The regular rate on grain carloads from Tignish, P.E.I., to St.

. John, is twenty-six cents per 100 pounds for 432 miles. From Tignish to Halifax it is twenty-three cents per 100 pounds for 309 miles; from Tignish to Sydney, twenty-six cents per 100 pounds for 308 miles. So you see that the farmers on the island are greatly handicapped on account of the excessive rates of freight. I believe that if this new route could be adopted there would not be any trouble. A company could be formed that would put a large car-carrying steamer on the route, and that would do away entirely with the three short hauls, because the large cars of the Intercolonial could be brought over and placed on the wharf and reloaded on island cars. This [DOT]would be a great convenience to our population over present conditions.

speechtext:
The importance of this subject to my province justifies me in making a few remarks. Year after year this House has listened to a discussion of this question, and it is still necessary to recur to it frequently. While I am pleased to say that some progress has been made during the last few years in giving us better transportation facilities, much remains to be done in that line. I think if this government put forth a little more effort and paid a little more attention to this question than thev have been doing, that without much expense they could considerably increase our transportation facilities. I will not say much as to the relative advantages of the different ports on. the mainland, because I do not pretend to have as much knowledge of the Brule route as those gentlemen possess who have made a special study of this question. But I want to tell the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), who I see is not in his seat, that if there is one thing upon which the people of Prince Edward Island are united, it is in the opinion that the Pictou harbour is the poorest harbour on the mainland for winter navigation. Let the government make no mistake on that point. The hon. member for Pictou almost taunted us to-night because we were not unanimous upon any route; but we are unanimous in the belief that the Pictou harbour offers the poorest harbour for winter navigation of any that can be mentioned. Let the government take that much for granted. Then I trust they will go on and make a good survey, and obtain sufficient knowledge to enable them to give us a better harbour. This is not my opinion only. I have studied the records and the reports of the surveyors that have been sent down by this government and by other governments, and I find there is a unanimous expression of opinion from these surveyors in their reports that Pictou harbour, on account of its shape and its situation, is certainly the least feasible
on the mainland for winter navigation. It is a V-shaped harbour, opening towards the northeast, and without any protection whatever. When the northeast and easterly winds blow the ice into that harbour, the whole harbour is blocked with ice, and navigation is completely stopped.
As to whether the people of Prince Edward Island are entitled to continuous navigation with the mainland, I do not think that question needs to be debated to-night. I was surprised on a recent occasion to hear the Minister of Finance, who I regret is not in his seat, though he seldom is absent, express the opinion that he did not believe it was binding on this government or on any government to give us continuous communication with the mainland. But I believe it is. The obligation is surely in our contract, and it would not be there if it was not meant to be valid. It surely must mean something or it would not be there, and if it means anything, it means that this government is obliged to give us continuous communication with the mainland in winter and in summer. A large percentage of the people of Prince Edward Island are united on this point also, that a tunnel will be the only complete and satisfactory solution' of the difficulty. When this subject was before the House on a previous occasion, the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) promised as much perhaps as he could in anything, that during the coming summer, or in the near future, and of the advisability and possibility of the tunnel would be thoroughly gone into. Speaking on behalf of those who have placed their hopes of the solution of this difficulty in the construction of a tunnel, I hope and trust that this government will, at an early day, make a proper survey of the Straits of Northumberland with a view to having a tunnel constructed if possible. This would obviate the difficulty we have in winter navigation.	[DOT]
Our difficulties of winter navigation are not our only difficulties. We have at present great drawbacks in our summer navigation. At present, the transportation of our mails and passengers and of a great deal of our freight is in the hands of a concern called the Steam Navigation Company. The people of Prince Edward Island, in the last few years, have become dissatisfied with the rates and with the service of that company. For my part, speaking as a passenger, I have no fault to find with the passenger service given by that company. But the rates charged and the facilities offered for transportation of freight are not up to date and not such as will satisfy the people. So that to-day a large percentage of the people of Prince Edward Island are thoroughly dissatisfied with the summer navigation of the Straits of Northumberland as conducted by the Steam

Navigation Company-almost as large a percentage as are dissatisfied with the winter navigation. And, as the hon. member for Queens county (Mr. Warburton) has said, I hope that when tenders are again called for, this matter will be earnestly considered by this government, with a view to giving the people better transportation rates and facilities.
I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. E. M. Macdonald) say, as I understood him, that the solution, of the difficulty would be to send all steamers from the mainland in the morning and get them back in the evening. That, as I understood him, would solve the question of the navigation of the straits in winter.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not take up the time of the House in discussing this- matter. As a matter of fact, I had not anticipated taking any part in the discussion, and would not

but for some observations that were made. I -desire to call the attention of the government and of the House to the fact that there is still another -route that has not been emphasized by hon. gentlemen who have spoken, a route that I claim will furnish a solution of the whole difficulty. It is idle to say that there is no grievance, that the people of the island are satisfied. All one has to do is to look at the ' Hansards ' ever since Prince Edward Island became a part of confederation and he will find year after year complaint on the part of the people of the island because of the treatment they were receiving in the matter of winter communication particularly. In the mass of information that was brought down last session, the session before last and in previous sessions, you will find resolutions of the Charlottetown Board of Trade, of the Maritime Board of Trade, of the Halifax Board of Trade, of the legislature of the province of Prince Edward Island, all bemoaning the treatment that Prince Edward Island was accorded in the matter of communication. The difficulty should be easily solved. It is a question of what is the best route, of ascertaining which is the most feasible route to maintain communication. Several routes have been tested. The Capes route, to which reference has been made by the hon. member for Prince, has been tested and has been declared to be ' a political and not a practical route.' There was a great deal of information brought down two years ago in reference to that route. Tests were made in the winter seasons of 1901, in 1902, and in 1903, and after it was tested the route had to be abandoned. Then, you have in summer time, the Charlottetown and Pietou route. When navigation closes, Charlottetown has to -be abandoned, and it struck me as rather extraordinary when I heard my hon. friend from Queens advocating the Charlottetown-Brule route. If the Charlottetown-Pictou route has to be abandoned as soon as winter opens, how is the Charlottetown-Brule route going to meet the requirements? If Charlotteown is not available as a winter port, then I contend that connecting it with Brule or Tatamagouche bay, is not going to better the situation.

maintopic: WINTER COMMUNICATION WITH PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND.
speechtext: The northern ice that is driven down the straits by the northeast wind is stopped up short at Point Prim, ten miles east of Charlottetown, and it does not interfere with the Charlottetown route.

maintopic: WINTER COMMUNICATION WITH PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND.
speechtext:
CHISHOLM Yes; but as I read the documents that have been brought down upon this subiect, they state that Charlottetown is not a good winter port. On the contrary, it is very much the opposite.
It is approached by a long, winding, nar-Mr. W. CHISHOLM. *
row channel, and although they have spent a great deal of money in the way of improvements and aids to navigation, and have done a great deal to improve Charlottetown harbour, it is conceded on all sides that Georgetown is the only winter port on the island. It is true that this year they have been running between Charlottetown and Pietou late in the season, and perhaps up to this date, but at any moment Georgetown is liable to be substituted for Charlottetown. Every one admits that Georgetown is one of the hest harbours in Prince Edward Island. No one has every thrown any -doubt upon the fact that Georgetown is open the whole winter long. The winter port on the island side is Georgetown. What you want to do is to test the various routes suggested by speakers -on this subject and adopt whatever route proves to be the best. I submit that as far as Brule, or Tatamagouche bay, is concerned, we have not very much to hope for there because the conditions, if I understood the Minister of Marine last year aright, are very much the same as those which are found in Pi-ctou harbour, and it would take an immense amount of money to have piers built and provide the accommodations that will be necessary, and even then it is very doubtful if a satisfactory winter route -can be found. There is, however, another route, the route which I suggest, and it is the Georgetown-Cape George route. This is a most desirable route by reason of the fact that there is plenty of sea room, and by reason of the condition of the tides and currents between Georgetown and Cape George ensuring open water all the year round. Three years ago, some time in March or April, when Pietou harbour was blocked for about ten days and was inaccessible, a. schooner laden with coal went from Hastings across to Georgetown, and I am told by sea captains and people who have spent all their lives along the coast, that Cape George has at all times open water. Two years ago when the ex-member for Kings, Prince Edward Island, was coming up here to Ottawa he was detained five or six days at Pietou harbour, while there was no difficulty about landing along the coast near Cape George.	This is not a new route. This
was suggested as far back as 1874 by the hon. member representing Kings at that time (Mr. McIntyre). He stated, what is generally conceded in the locality, that there is always open water between Georgetown and Cape George. During that same session the then member for Ant-igonish county (Mr. Mclsaac) pointed out that to his own knowledge, passengers had been landed at Malignant Cove. Arisaig and Cape George, when they could not get near Pietou. I know that a few years ago, when Pietou harbour was inaccessible, they had
3205*

to land their passengers and mails somewhere near Cape George. I wish to direct the attention of the government to the necessity of properly testing this George-town-Cape George route, and if it is found to be what we claim for it, by all means adopt it. A promise was made by the late Minister of Marine and Fisheries, in a letter to me, dated November 3, 1905, that this route would be tested at the proper time. I had a similar promise from the present minister, whose absence we all regret, in a letter dated the 28th August, 1906, in which I called his attention to the rumour in the newspapers that there was a test to be made of the Brule route. He promised then that he would see that the Georgetown-Oape George route was tested when the proper time ,came. In view of what has been done in the way of surveys of Tatamagouche bay, I think the time has come when the promise of the minister should be taken seriously to heart. Representations have been made regarding the proposed route on the floor of this House time and again, almost as far back as 1874. These representations were made by the member for Kings to whom I referred, by the member for An-tigonish, my predecessor, and by his predecessor. I think that these representations and the representations made by me to the department verbally and in writing are sufficient to justify a test being made,, and I hope as I sincerely believe the government will carry out the promise that was made bv the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and his predecessor and have this test made as soon as possible.
Motion agreed to.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-CO-OPERATIVE LOAN AND CREDIT BANKS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before ti e House adjourns I would like to ask the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) if it would not be possible to give a second reading to Bill (No. 26) on Co-operative Loan and Credit Banks. The reason 1 am asking this is that throughout the course of the discussion on the first Bill presented respecting co-operation, the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) will remember, that there was no objection whatever as to the feature of co-operation. There was strenuous objection to productive and distributive co-operative societies, but no objection was made at any stage of the Bill to small banks, and loan and credit societies. Under these circumstances this year I presented a Bill for the purpose of legally organizing loan and credit societies feeling certain that upon that feature at
any rate there would be no opposition whatever. The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Harris) has presented a general, comprehensive co-operative Bill which, I understand, is opposed by certain interests, but there are no interests whatever that have any such opposition to these credit banks. They have been approved of by the bankers association. Under these circumstances and as that feature of cooperation has developed very much in the province of Quebec principally, and as there has been no objection to the first Bill in regard to that particular aspect of it. I think my request commends itself to the right hon. the Prime Minister. If my Bill were read a second time now and even a third time, if possibly there is any opposition, it might be offered in the Senate.

speechtext: I understand it is the wish of the House that this Bill should be considered, I have no objection at all that it should be read a second time and submitted to the committee, I cannot agree that it should be read a third time because I know there are some persons who want to be heard in opposition to it. I withdraw my motion that the House adjourn.
